newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical groups to show strong 9-mo profits.
newsitem.headline: German chemical groups to show strong 9-mo profits.

text.p: Germany's largest chemical groups, reaping the benefits of a softer mark, will likely show double digit profit growth in the first nine months of 1996, but analysts said overall business conditions were mixed.

"One factor supporting the chemical industry's results in the first nine months will be the weaker mark," making German exports more attractive abroad, said Christiane Dienhart, analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich.
Bayer AG will kick off the triumvirate's reporting season on November 5 with Hoechst AG following on November 6 and BASF AG reporting on November 13.
Analysts forecast Bayer's nine-month pre-tax profit ranged between 3.68 and 3.78 billion marks, showing an average 13 percent rise.
Sales meanwhile were said to have grown at an average 7.3 percent rate, ranging between 36.24 and 36.75 billion marks.
A year ago Bayer reported nine-month pre-tax profit at 3.304 billion marks and sales at 34.027 billion marks.
For Hoechst, whose 1996 results have been significantly shaped by extraordinary earnings, analysts forecast only third quarter pre-tax profits excluding extraordinary earnings.

The estimates ranged between 802 million marks and 1.5 billion marks compared with last year's 3.426 billion mark level. "But the numbers really cannot be compared since there are so many uncertainties about the extraordinaries," said one analyst asking not to be named.
Similarly forecasts for sales, ranging between 38.6 and 39.0 billion marks, were also difficult to make, analysts said, adding they would likely be below last year's 39.14 billion mark turnover.
At BASF analysts saw an average 11 percent rise in pre-tax profits ranging between 3.41 and 3.51 billion marks with sales, excluding taxes, ranging between 33.56 and 33.75 billion marks.
This marks only a small increase from last year's 35.117 billion mark turnover. Including taxes, BASF's 1995 nine-month turnover stood at 37.44 billion marks.

After grappling with the negative effects of a strong mark in 1995, the chemical industry now appears freed of the currency problem, able to boost exports analysts said, adding sales in Asia and North America likely spearheaded growth.
"The reviving economy will also have an impact on results," said Peter Mackey, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

Similarly analysts said the groups may have been able to push through selected price increases as well as receiving some support from higher oil prices. "Especially at BASF, higher oil prices will have supported results," Mackey added.
On the other hand the industry still faces difficult conditions in the fibres and plastics markets, analysts said, cautioning strong headline results figures may not tell the industry's whole story.

Analysts said they would be eyeing Hoechst in particular after the company said its pre-tax profit more than doubled to 4.3 billion marks in the first six months of the year. But that number also included 2.1 billion marks of extraordinary income from the sale of several units, including SGL Carbon AG.

Several analysts said it would be interesting to see how AgrEvo, the group's crop protection unit it runs jointly with Schering AG, will affect results, particularly since AgrEvo already announced strong nine month results.
All three companies will detail results at news conferences.
